_meta.governance: Curated additive risk table per SCORING_METHODOLOGY.md §5. Tiers reflect RISK (real-world dietary exposure vs regulatory intake limits), not theoretical hazard. Every entry cites a named regulatory review (EFSA, FDA, JECFA, IARC) — never blogs or single cherry-picked studies. Keys match Open Food Facts additives_tags format (en:eXXX). Changes to this table increment the score_version; log changes in MEMORY.md. Additives not present in this table are scored as low tier and flagged as 'not yet reviewed' in the score detail — absence of review is never treated as evidence of concern.

tiers.low: Broadly recognized as safe at typical intakes; no penalty.
tiers.moderate: Regulatory intake caution exists (ADI set, some groups may approach it, or labeling requirements apply).
tiers.higher: Restricted or withdrawn in at least one major jurisdiction, or under active regulatory re-review with unresolved concerns.

en:e100.name: Curcumin
en:e100.reason: Natural turmeric color; EFSA set an ADI and typical dietary exposure stays within it.

sources.name: EFSA re-evaluation of curcumin (E100), 2010

en:e101.name: Riboflavin (vitamin B2)
en:e101.reason: A B vitamin used as a yellow color; EFSA found no safety concern at reported uses.

sources.name: EFSA re-evaluation of riboflavins (E101), 2013

en:e102.name: Tartrazine
en:e102.reason: Azo color with an EFSA ADI; foods containing it in the EU must carry a note about possible effects on activity and attention in children.

sources.name: EFSA re-evaluation of tartrazine (E102), 2009
EU Regulation 1333/2008 Annex V (labelling of certain colours)

en:e104.name: Quinoline yellow
en:e104.reason: EFSA lowered its ADI in 2009 and EU labelling rules for certain colors apply; not authorized for food in the US.

sources.name: EFSA re-evaluation of quinoline yellow (E104), 2009

en:e110.name: Sunset yellow FCF
en:e110.reason: Azo color; EFSA revised its ADI in 2014 and EU child-activity labelling rules apply.

sources.name: EFSA refined exposure assessment of sunset yellow (E110), 2014

en:e120.name: Cochineal / carminic acid (carmine)
en:e120.reason: EFSA maintained the ADI in 2015; rare hypersensitivity reactions are documented, so people with known sensitivity may want to check for it.

sources.name: EFSA re-evaluation of cochineal, carminic acid, carmines (E120), 2015

en:e122.name: Azorubine / carmoisine
en:e122.reason: Azo color with an EFSA ADI; EU child-activity labelling rules apply and it is not authorized in the US.

sources.name: EFSA re-evaluation of azorubine/carmoisine (E122), 2009

en:e124.name: Ponceau 4R
en:e124.reason: EFSA lowered its ADI in 2009; EU child-activity labelling rules apply and it is not authorized in the US.

sources.name: EFSA re-evaluation of Ponceau 4R (E124), 2009

en:e127.name: Erythrosine (Red 3)
en:e127.reason: The US FDA revoked its authorization for foods in January 2025 based on findings in laboratory animals; it remains permitted in limited uses elsewhere.

sources.name: FDA order revoking authorization of FD&C Red No. 3, 2025
EFSA re-evaluation of erythrosine (E127), 2011

en:e129.name: Allura red AC
en:e129.reason: Azo color with an EFSA ADI; EU child-activity labelling rules apply.

sources.name: EFSA re-evaluation of Allura Red AC (E129), 2009

en:e133.name: Brilliant blue FCF
en:e133.reason: EFSA set an ADI and estimated dietary exposure stays below it for all population groups.

sources.name: EFSA re-evaluation of Brilliant Blue FCF (E133), 2010

en:e150d.name: Sulphite ammonia caramel
en:e150d.reason: EFSA set a group ADI for caramel colors; the 4-MEI byproduct is monitored and intake by high consumers can approach the ADI.

sources.name: EFSA re-evaluation of caramel colours (E150a-d), 2011

en:e160a.name: Carotenes
en:e160a.reason: Plant-derived orange pigments (provitamin A); EFSA found reported food uses of mixed carotenes to be of no safety concern.

sources.name: EFSA re-evaluation of mixed carotenes (E160a), 2012

en:e160b.name: Annatto extracts
en:e160b.reason: Seed-derived color; EFSA set updated ADIs in 2016 and exposure estimates stay within them.

sources.name: EFSA safety assessment of annatto extracts (E160b), 2016

en:e160c.name: Paprika extract
en:e160c.reason: Pepper-derived color; EFSA found no safety concern at reported use levels.

sources.name: EFSA re-evaluation of paprika extract (E160c), 2015

en:e170.name: Calcium carbonate
en:e170.reason: A mineral (chalk) also used as a calcium source; EFSA found no safety concern at reported uses.

sources.name: EFSA re-evaluation of calcium carbonate (E170), 2011

en:e171.name: Titanium dioxide
en:e171.reason: EFSA concluded in 2021 that genotoxicity could not be ruled out and the EU withdrew its food authorization in 2022; it remains permitted in some other jurisdictions, including the US.

sources.name: EFSA safety assessment of titanium dioxide (E171), 2021
EU Regulation 2022/63 (removal of E171 from authorized additives)

en:e202.name: Potassium sorbate
en:e202.reason: Common preservative; EFSA set a revised group ADI in 2019 and typical exposure stays within it.

sources.name: EFSA revised group ADI for sorbic acid and potassium sorbate (E200, E202), 2019

en:e211.name: Sodium benzoate
en:e211.reason: Preservative with an EFSA group ADI; intake by children who consume many soft drinks can approach the ADI, and benzene can form in some drinks that also contain vitamin C.

sources.name: EFSA re-evaluation of benzoic acid and benzoates (E210-E213), 2016

en:e220.name: Sulphur dioxide
en:e220.reason: EFSA's 2022 re-evaluation could not confirm the safety of the previous ADI due to data gaps, and some people are sensitive to sulphites; it must be declared as an allergen in the EU and US.

sources.name: EFSA re-evaluation of sulphur dioxide and sulphites (E220-E228), 2022

en:e249.name: Potassium nitrite
en:e249.reason: Curing salt for processed meats; EFSA's 2023 assessment found dietary exposure to nitrosamines, which can form from nitrites, raises a health concern across age groups.

sources.name: EFSA opinion on nitrosamines in food, 2023
IARC Monographs vol. 114 (processed meat), 2015

en:e250.name: Sodium nitrite
en:e250.reason: Curing salt for processed meats; EFSA's 2023 assessment found dietary exposure to nitrosamines, which can form from nitrites, raises a health concern, and the EU tightened permitted levels in 2023.

sources.name: EFSA opinion on nitrosamines in food, 2023
EU Regulation 2023/2108 (lower limits for nitrites and nitrates)

en:e251.name: Sodium nitrate
en:e251.reason: Can convert to nitrite in the body; EFSA re-confirmed the ADI in 2017 but the EU lowered permitted use levels in 2023 as a precaution around nitrosamine formation.

sources.name: EFSA re-evaluation of sodium and potassium nitrate (E251-E252), 2017
EU Regulation 2023/2108 (lower limits for nitrites and nitrates)

en:e260.name: Acetic acid
en:e260.reason: The acid in vinegar; regulators place no numeric intake limit on it.

sources.name: JECFA evaluation of acetic acid (ADI not limited)

en:e270.name: Lactic acid
en:e270.reason: Naturally produced in fermentation; regulators place no numeric intake limit on it.

sources.name: JECFA evaluation of lactic acid (ADI not limited)

en:e296.name: Malic acid
en:e296.reason: Fruit acid found naturally in apples; regulators place no numeric intake limit on it.

sources.name: JECFA evaluation of malic acid (ADI not limited)

en:e300.name: Ascorbic acid (vitamin C)
en:e300.reason: Vitamin C used as an antioxidant; EFSA found no safety concern and no need for a numeric ADI.

sources.name: EFSA re-evaluation of ascorbic acid (E300-E302), 2015

en:e306.name: Tocopherol-rich extract (vitamin E)
en:e306.reason: Vitamin E used as an antioxidant; EFSA found no safety concern at reported uses.

sources.name: EFSA re-evaluation of tocopherols (E306-E309), 2015

en:e320.name: Butylated hydroxyanisole (BHA)
en:e320.reason: Synthetic antioxidant with an EFSA ADI; IARC classifies it as Group 2B (possibly carcinogenic, based on high-dose animal data) while typical dietary exposure stays below the ADI.

sources.name: EFSA re-evaluation of BHA (E320), 2011
IARC Monographs list of classifications (BHA, Group 2B)

en:e321.name: Butylated hydroxytoluene (BHT)
en:e321.reason: Synthetic antioxidant; EFSA set an ADI in 2012 and high consumers can approach it.

sources.name: EFSA re-evaluation of BHT (E321), 2012

en:e322.name: Lecithins
en:e322.reason: Emulsifier usually from soy or sunflower; EFSA found no safety concern at reported uses.

sources.name: EFSA re-evaluation of lecithins (E322), 2017

en:e330.name: Citric acid
en:e330.reason: Fruit acid found naturally in citrus; regulators place no numeric intake limit on it.

sources.name: JECFA evaluation of citric acid (ADI not limited)

en:e331.name: Sodium citrates
en:e331.reason: Salts of citric acid used to regulate acidity; regulators place no numeric intake limit on them.

sources.name: JECFA evaluation of citrates (ADI not limited)

en:e338.name: Phosphoric acid
en:e338.reason: EFSA set a group intake limit for phosphates in 2019 and estimated that high consumers, especially children and teens, can exceed it.

sources.name: EFSA re-evaluation of phosphoric acid and phosphates (E338-E341, E343, E450-E452), 2019

en:e406.name: Agar
en:e406.reason: Seaweed-derived gelling agent; EFSA found no safety concern at reported uses.

sources.name: EFSA re-evaluation of agar (E406), 2016

en:e407.name: Carrageenan
en:e407.reason: Seaweed-derived thickener; EFSA kept a temporary ADI in 2018 because of data gaps and asked for further studies.

sources.name: EFSA re-evaluation of carrageenan (E407), 2018

en:e410.name: Locust bean gum
en:e410.reason: Carob-seed thickener; EFSA found no safety concern for the general population at reported uses.

sources.name: EFSA re-evaluation of locust bean gum (E410), 2017

en:e412.name: Guar gum
en:e412.reason: Plant-seed thickener; EFSA found no safety concern at reported uses.

sources.name: EFSA re-evaluation of guar gum (E412), 2017

en:e415.name: Xanthan gum
en:e415.reason: Fermentation-derived thickener; EFSA found no safety concern at reported uses.

sources.name: EFSA re-evaluation of xanthan gum (E415), 2017

en:e422.name: Glycerol
en:e422.reason: Humectant naturally present in fats; EFSA found no safety concern at reported uses.

sources.name: EFSA re-evaluation of glycerol (E422), 2017

en:e433.name: Polysorbate 80
en:e433.reason: Emulsifier with an EFSA group ADI; EFSA noted data gaps at re-evaluation and research on emulsifier effects on the gut is ongoing.

sources.name: EFSA re-evaluation of polysorbates (E432-E436), 2015

en:e440.name: Pectins
en:e440.reason: Fruit-derived gelling agent; EFSA found no safety concern and no need for a numeric ADI.

sources.name: EFSA re-evaluation of pectins (E440i, E440ii), 2017

en:e450.name: Diphosphates
en:e450.reason: Part of the phosphate group for which EFSA set a group intake limit in 2019; high consumers can exceed it.

sources.name: EFSA re-evaluation of phosphoric acid and phosphates (E338-E341, E343, E450-E452), 2019

en:e466.name: Carboxymethylcellulose (cellulose gum)
en:e466.reason: EFSA found no safety concern at re-evaluation but noted data gaps, and research on emulsifier effects on the gut microbiome is ongoing.

sources.name: EFSA re-evaluation of celluloses including E466, 2018

en:e471.name: Mono- and diglycerides of fatty acids
en:e471.reason: Emulsifiers digested like ordinary dietary fats; EFSA found no safety concern at reported uses.

sources.name: EFSA re-evaluation of mono- and diglycerides (E471), 2017

en:e500.name: Sodium carbonates (baking soda)
en:e500.reason: Common raising agent; regulators place no numeric intake limit on it.

sources.name: JECFA evaluation of sodium carbonates (ADI not limited)

en:e621.name: Monosodium glutamate (MSG)
en:e621.reason: EFSA set a group ADI for glutamates in 2017 and estimated that some population groups can exceed it; glutamate is otherwise a normal component of protein-rich foods.

sources.name: EFSA re-evaluation of glutamic acid and glutamates (E620-E625), 2017

en:e924.name: Potassium bromate
en:e924.reason: Flour treatment agent withdrawn from food use in the EU, UK, and Canada; IARC classifies it as Group 2B based on animal studies, and it remains permitted with limits in some jurisdictions.

sources.name: IARC Monographs list of classifications (potassium bromate, Group 2B)

en:e950.name: Acesulfame K
en:e950.reason: Sweetener with an EFSA ADI that typical intakes stay within; the WHO's 2023 guideline advises against relying on non-sugar sweeteners for weight management.

sources.name: EFSA re-evaluation of acesulfame K (E950), 2025
WHO guideline on non-sugar sweeteners, 2023

en:e951.name: Aspartame
en:e951.reason: EFSA and JECFA maintain an ADI that typical intakes stay well within; IARC classified it Group 2B (limited evidence) in 2023, which JECFA reviewed without changing the ADI.

sources.name: EFSA full risk assessment of aspartame, 2013
IARC/JECFA joint statement on aspartame, 2023

en:e955.name: Sucralose
en:e955.reason: Sweetener with a JECFA/EFSA ADI that typical intakes stay within; the WHO's 2023 guideline advises against relying on non-sugar sweeteners for weight management and EFSA re-evaluation is ongoing.

sources.name: EFSA sweeteners re-evaluation programme
WHO guideline on non-sugar sweeteners, 2023
